slides.title: How many people does it take to build one cluster?
slides.transcript:
How many roofs does it take to cover one computer?

At Meta, the team building an AI training cluster started with a reasonable assumption. All those machines could work together under one roof. Then came Prometheus. More than thirty structures, spread across different locations. Suddenly you need someone who understands fiber, someone who knows the buildings, and someone who can get all those people talking.

Now picture the crowd at the Open Compute Project Global Summit. Forty-four hundred people in 2023. More than seven thousand the next year. Nearly eleven thousand in 2025. In 2026, fifteen thousand people came to San Jose.

Some design chips. Some run facilities. Some ask who’s going to pay for it all. As you meet a few of them, keep one seat at the table in mind. Who would you bring?

slides.title: What does OCP count?
slides.transcript:
Picture a purchase order on a desk. A data center operator needs servers for a new hall. The operator pays an equipment supplier. A shared design helped shape those servers. Where, exactly, does that purchase show up?

OCP commissioned IDC to study what buyers around the world spend on equipment based on OCP-recognized designs. Servers account for the largest part. The study also covers equipment such as switches, racks, power systems and cooling. Think of the dollars as traveling from a buyer to a seller. That’s the transaction the study is trying to measure.

Here’s an interesting wrinkle. A company can use an openly shared design even if it has never joined OCP. The design can travel farther than the membership list. That’s part of what makes the market worth measuring. And in 2026, the people doing the measuring had quite an update.

options.label: The supplier
options.text: The supplier receives payment for the equipment. IDC measures spending on these transactions worldwide.

options.label: The shared design
options.text: A drawing or specification helps teams build or choose equipment. The equipment purchase is what IDC counts.

slides.title: The forecast that moved
slides.transcript:
In 2023, the opening address at the Global Summit picked up on a change. AI was already prompting the industry to rethink how much data center infrastructure it would need.

A year later, IDC put a number on one part of that story. Its 2024 study projected seventy-three and a half billion dollars in spending on OCP-recognized equipment in 2028.

Now move the target year forward once, to 2029. Leave it there. In the 2025 study, IDC expected buyers to spend two hundred ninety-five billion dollars that year.

Imagine you’re at the next Summit, waiting for the new estimate. Move the marker to where you think it landed. Make your guess.

About eight hundred billion dollars. Same target year. About two point seven times the earlier forecast. IDC points to two changes. Buyers are investing more in AI infrastructure, and OCP designs are finding their way into more of that equipment.

One year further out, IDC projects eight hundred ninety-two billion dollars in 2030. That would be about fifty-one percent of spending across the categories the study measures. When you hear that number repeated, take the year and the scope along with it.

slides.title: What does a shared design buy a team?
slides.transcript:
A rack is on order. The delivery date is circled. The facilities lead has a question. Will the new equipment work with what’s already in the room?

One way to lose a week is to discover that question on the loading dock. With a shared drawing, the buyer, the installer and the facilities lead can sit down together while there’s still time to change the plan. They can check clearances, ask which connections have been tested, and agree on who will support the installation.

A separate study by SG Strategy asked organizations about the value they get from taking part in OCP. It reported that infrastructure deployment could be accelerated by up to fifteen percent. The number describes a range of experience. The conversation on the loading dock is one way to picture what saved time might look like.

Think about your own team. Which question would you most like answered before delivery day?

activity.prompt: What would you check before delivery?

options.label: Room to work
options.text: Ask for the service clearances. A rack can fit the floor plan and still leave too little room to replace a tray.

options.label: Connections
options.text: Give the installation team the interface drawings early. Confirm which combinations have been tested.

options.label: Support
options.text: Agree on who owns the issue when it crosses two suppliers’ equipment. Put those contacts in the handover.

slides.section_label: Three moments from the Summit floor
slides.title: What can another team build from this rack?
slides.transcript:
At the Summit, AMD’s Lisa Su described a choice her team made for Helios. They used Open Rack Wide. On stage, she traced the work back to the partners, including Meta, who helped turn the rack architecture into something customers could use. The power shelves and the way the equipment is managed are part of that story, too.

Now look at a different rack. Ian Buck walked through the rack and tray designs NVIDIA was contributing through MGX 1.2. Watch the tray slide toward the back of the rack. Think about the person who has to reach those connections when a tray needs service.

A buyer and a technician can look at the very same drawing and notice different things. The buyer wants to know which suppliers can work to the interface. The technician wants to know how the connection comes apart on a Tuesday night when the system is in use. Choose a perspective and see what catches your eye.

slides.section_label: Three moments from the Summit floor
slides.title: When a cluster outgrows its roof
slides.transcript:
Come back to Prometheus. Inside one building, the computers already have to exchange information quickly enough to work as a team. Now put some of those computers in another building. The training job still needs them to act like one cluster.

Santosh Janardhan described how Meta brought connections from different buildings together in a regional network. Follow the light from one roof to the next. Along the way, somebody has to specify the fiber, choose the switches and figure out what happens if a path goes down.

Bloomberg Intelligence sees that change in the market around each AI rack. Adding computers also creates demand for the equipment that connects them. A network designer can look at a map like this and see a whole second shopping list.

Pick a link between the buildings. What would you want to know before that link became part of a training run?

options.label: Between buildings
options.text: Distance matters. A team needs fiber routes and switching equipment to carry traffic from one roof to the next.

options.label: Across sites
options.text: Ask how the network brings paths together and what happens when a link fails. Listen to Meta’s regional network example.

slides.section_label: Three moments from the Summit floor
slides.title: What if the next supplier’s connector fits?
slides.transcript:
You’ve found room for another rack. Your usual supplier has a long lead time. A second supplier says its equipment will fit. What would you like them to send you?

In their power keynote, ABB and Eaton used the example of a connector. An electrical system can stay in service through several generations of computing equipment. A shared interface gives the people designing the next generation something concrete to work with.

Follow the power path into the rack. Here, where two pieces meet, a drawing gives both teams a way to check the dimensions and the electrical requirements. Then they can ask which combinations have actually been tested.

IDC describes a practical advantage for buyers when parts are scarce. With a shared specification, they have somewhere to start when they look for a second source.

You’re the buyer. Pick what you’d request first. See which question it helps you answer.

slides.title: Would you run that headline?
slides.transcript:
You’re on the editor’s desk. Three headlines have arrived, and only one gets the forecast right. Look for the buyer, the target year and the word that tells you this is still a prediction.

Then take a call from a second supplier. They have a part for your rack. Pick the two requests that would help you decide whether it fits and works. Submit both questions to continue. You can try again after the feedback, and any completed attempt takes you forward.

slides.section_label: Where will you take this in 2027?
slides.title: Where should the answer come from?
slides.transcript:
Picture a camera above a moving production line. A bottle passes underneath. The camera spots a crooked cap. A machine downstream has a moment to divert the bottle. Where should the image go for an answer?

One path leads to a computer beside the line. The other leads to a remote data center. Give the remote path a little more distance and you can see why the team might want to try running the model on site. But who will service the local computer? And how much space and cooling will it need?

This is inference, putting a trained model to work on a new input. OCP’s AI Computing Continuum Project, or AICC, works on open hardware for places like this factory. A computer beside the line has to fit the space, power and cooling the factory can spare.

At the Summit, OCP’s George Tchaparian asked for help on three fronts as the community looks to 2027. Give designers more choice of AI chips. Design the computing equipment and its facility together. And make open infrastructure useful wherever inference needs to happen, including places like this factory.

Which question would you ask the factory team first?

options.label: When is the answer due?
options.text: Time the journey from camera to decision. Could the line divert the product before it passes the gate?

options.label: Who maintains the computer?
options.text: A local installation needs someone who can service it. The available space, cooling and support shape the choice.

slides.section_label: Where will you take this in 2027?
slides.title: Find your first conversation
slides.transcript:
Start with something you already know. If you buy or maintain equipment, the Rack and Power Project is a place to bring a detail you wish had been on a supplier’s drawing. If you connect buildings, the Networking Project is a place to compare notes on what changes when a cluster moves beyond one site.

If economics or policy is your field, take a look at Heat Reuse. A data center may have heat to offer. A neighbor may have a use for it. People still have to work out who pays for the connection and what happens when demand changes. There are workstreams for exactly those questions.

And if you run a factory, an enterprise site or a telecom facility, the AI Computing Continuum Project wants to understand where equipment will actually have to work.

Pick the conversation you’d like to try. You’ll find a question to start with and a link to the people already working on it.

slides.section_label: Where will you take this in 2027?
slides.title: While the Summit lights were coming down
slides.transcript:
When OCP looked back on the Academy’s first year at the October Summit, more than six thousand learners had registered. Together they’d logged more than thirty thousand hours.

By November 2026, the Academy had grown to more than eight thousand users and almost forty thousand learner hours. Think of one of those hours. Someone is getting ready for a project call. They’d like to understand the drawing before they ask their first question.

If the rack examples caught your interest, look for Open Rack in the Data Center Technologies catalog. If you followed the heat, try Introduction to Liquid Cooling. You can open the catalog from here and choose the subject that brings you a little closer to the conversation.

slides.section_label: Where will you take this in 2027?
slides.title: What will you bring?
slides.transcript:
What stayed with you? The forecast that changed by hundreds of billions of dollars? The network that let buildings miles apart work on one problem? Or that small connection at the back of a rack that two suppliers have to get right?

Each started with a question someone could ask. You probably have one of your own. Pick a project, look up the next call, and bring the question that keeps coming up at work. If you’d like to follow along first, subscribe to the OCP newsletter. And whenever you want to get comfortable with a new subject, the Data Center Technologies catalog is there for you.

Thank you for spending this time with OCP Academy. I hope we hear your question in 2027.
